description:
Astro-Twin: a digital twin that shows astronauts their health at a glance 

Hi! I'm Luis Alegria, a electrical and computer engineering student at Bunker Hill Community College, who loves space and building things that make complex data easy to understand. I'm entering Space Apps 2026 with Astro-Twin, a web app that turns astronaut health data into an interactive body map. Each part of the body glows green, yellow or red based on its readings.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Astro-Twin is a web app that turns astronaut health data into an interactive "digital twin." An avatar is split into four regions:

  • the head (brain and vision);
  • the torso (heart and blood);
  • the limbs (bone and muscle);
  • a surrounding field (radiation and immune health).

Each region is colored green (normal), yellow (caution) or red (critical) according to its worst reading. Clicking a region opens a dashboard with each value, its limits and a plain-language explanation. Systems are listed most severe first, so the biggest problem is always at the top.

The app has three modes:

  1. Scenario: a mission astronaut on the ISS, Moon or Mars. The app stores only the measured values and works out each status from limits for the chosen environment, so the same reading can change color between environments. Partial gravity relaxes the limits for head and eye readings. On Mars, critical readings also warn that the ~22-minute signal delay to Earth means the crew must respond on their own.
  2. NASA Data: real Inspiration4 crew blood work from NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSD-569 and OSD-575), which now hosts the Life Sciences Data Archive. Users pick a crew member and play back 7 test dates, from 92 days before launch to 194 days after return. Each value is graded against the lab's own normal range. Values that look like data-entry errors are flagged "Data check" instead of raising false alarms.
  3. Cognitive Lab: blood work can't measure the brain, so we built three short games based on standard thinking tests:
  • Reaction Time (alertness);
  • Symbol Match (processing speed);
  • Memory Grid (visual working memory). Scores are compared with a pre-flight baseline, plotted on a mission timeline, and feed the avatar's head.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

As missions move toward the Moon and Mars, crews can't rely on real-time help from flight surgeons on Earth. Astro-Twin turns scattered lab panels and test scores into one picture an astronaut can understand in seconds, without medical training. It aims to support crew decisions far from Earth. It could also serve as a teaching tool that shows students and the public how spaceflight affects the body.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

  • It treats the human body like a spacecraft's status display, a format astronauts already know.
  • One color system covers real NASA data, mission scenarios and live game scores.
  • Health limits change with the environment, which connects physiology to mission design.
  • The brain-game "check-in" fills a gap in the available data instead of leaving it blank.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

  • Languages: JavaScript (React 18), HTML, CSS
  • Frameworks and tools: Vite, Tailwind CSS, Lucide icons, Node.js (data conversion script), Git and GitHub
  • Data: NASA OSDR / ALSDA Inspiration4 Complete Blood Count and Comprehensive Metabolic Panel tables; NASA Human Research Program and NASA-STD-3001 as references
  • Hardware: none needed. It runs in any modern web browser, on desktop or tablet.
  • AI assistance: Claude Code (Anthropic) was used as a coding assistant during development.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

  • Honesty about data: every screen labels what is real NASA data, what is a mock value, and what is simulated. The environment limits are clearly marked as placeholders, to be replaced with NASA-STD-3001 values.
  • Medical caution: the cognitive games estimate thinking performance only. They are not a diagnosis or a measure of brain pressure.
  • Data quality: we checked the NASA files for suspect values instead of trusting them blindly.
  • Accessibility: status is shown with text labels as well as color, and the avatar can be used with a keyboard.
  • Privacy: the NASA data is de-identified, and game scores are stored only in the user's own browser.
  • Reproducibility: the raw NASA files and the conversion script are in the public repo, and every source is linked in the README.

NEXT STEPS

  • Replace the placeholder limits with sourced NASA-STD-3001 and HRP values.
  • Add inputs for onboard eye scans, optic-nerve ultrasound and eye-pressure readings.
  • Add daily habit rings to encourage exercise, hydration and cognitive check-ins.
